name: Affine lines in the plane
questiontext:
A linear line in the plane is a one dimensional subspace of \(R^2\) of the form \(m = Span(v)\) where \(0 \ne v \in R^2\). An affine line is a translation of a linear line; obtained by adding one constant vector \(\ell : m + w_1 = \{\alpha v + w_1 \ | \ \alpha \in R\}\). In the picture we see how we can replace \(w_1\) by a different point \(w_2\) on the same affine to obtain a new parametrization of the same line \(\ell: m+w2=\{\beta v + w_2 \ | \ \beta \in R\}\).

Two affine lines \(\ell_1 = w_1+Span(v_1), \ell_2 = w_2 + Span(v_2)\) can be in one of three possible mutual configurations (1) Parallel, (2) Intersecting, and (3) Coincident (namely they are the same line). The following pictures demonstrate these possibilities.

Consider the following lines

\[\ell_1: {{CT:0}}+Span \left( {{CT:1}} \right), \ell_2: {{CT:2}} + Span \left( {{CT:3}} \right) \]

generalfeedback:
Outline: Compare the direction vectors: independent directions in the plane mean the lines intersect; dependent directions mean parallel or coincident, and one point decides which (part a). The distance (part b) uses a vector orthogonal to the lines, and the cosine (part c) uses the inner product of the direction vectors.
Step 1 — The mutual configuration (part a)
The direction vectors are \(v_1={{CT:1}}\) and \(v_2={{CT:3}}\). They are linearly dependent exactly when the determinant of the matrix with columns \(v_1,v_2\) is zero:

\[ \det\left[\,v_1\ \ v_2\,\right]={{CT:4}} \]

[[if test="{{CT:23}}"]]The determinant is not zero, so \(v_1,v_2\) are linearly independent. Two lines in the plane with independent directions are not parallel, so they meet in exactly one point. Indeed, taking \(t={{CT:5}}\) on \(\ell_1\) and \(t={{CT:6}}\) on \(\ell_2\):

\[ {{CT:0}}+\left({{CT:5}}\right){{CT:1}}={{CT:7}}={{CT:2}}+\left({{CT:6}}\right){{CT:3}} \]

So the lines are intersecting:

\[ \ell_1\cap\ell_2=\left\{ {{CT:7}} \right\}\quad\Rightarrow\quad 2 \]

[[else]]The determinant is zero, so \(v_2={{CT:8}}\): the directions are parallel, and the lines are either parallel or coincident. They coincide exactly when \(w_2\in\ell_1\), that is, when \(w_2-w_1\) is a multiple of \(v_1\). Here

\[ w_2-w_1={{CT:9}},\qquad \det\left[\,w_2-w_1\ \ v_1\,\right]={{CT:10}}[[if test="{{CT:24}}"]]\ne 0[[/if]], \]

[[if test="{{CT:25}}"]]so \(w_2-w_1={{CT:11}}\) is a multiple of \(v_1\), that is, \(w_2=w_1+\left({{CT:5}}\right)v_1\in\ell_1\). The lines are coincident:

\[ \ell_1=\ell_2\quad\Rightarrow\quad 3 \]

[[else]]so \(w_2-w_1\) is not a multiple of \(v_1\), and \(w_2\notin\ell_1\). The lines are parallel and distinct:

\[ \ell_1\parallel\ell_2\quad\Rightarrow\quad 1 \]

[[/if]][[/if]]
Step 2 — The distance (part b)
[[if test="{{CT:23}}"]]The lines meet at the point \({{CT:7}}\), so the distance between them is zero:

\[ d(\ell_1,\ell_2)=0 \]

[[elif test="{{CT:25}}"]]The lines coincide, so the distance between them is zero:

\[ d(\ell_1,\ell_2)=0 \]

[[else]]For parallel lines, the distance is the length of the projection of \(w_2-w_1\) (a vector from a point of \(\ell_1\) to a point of \(\ell_2\)) on a direction orthogonal to both lines. Rotating \(v_1\) by 90 degrees gives such a direction:

\[ o={{CT:12}}{{CT:1}}={{CT:13}} \]

The length of the projection is \(\frac{|(w_2-w_1)\cdot o|}{\|o\|}\), with \((w_2-w_1)\cdot o={{CT:14}}\) and \(\|o\|={{CT:15}}\):

\[ d(\ell_1,\ell_2)=\frac{|{{CT:14}}|}{{{CT:15}}}={{CT:16}} \]

[[/if]]
Step 3 — The cosine of the angle (part c)
[[if test="{{CT:23}}"]]The angle between the lines is the angle between their direction vectors, so it is computed with the inner product:

\[ \cos\theta=\frac{v_1\cdot v_2}{\|v_1\|\,\|v_2\|}=\frac{{{CT:17}}}{{{CT:18}}\cdot {{CT:19}}}={{CT:20}} \]

A line has no preferred direction: replacing \(v_2\) by \(-v_2\) changes only the sign of the cosine. Therefore both \({{CT:21}}\) (the acute angle) and \({{CT:22}}\) are accepted:

\[ \cos\theta={{CT:21}} \]

[[else]]The direction vectors are parallel, so the angle between the lines is 0, and as instructed we enter 1 (indeed \(v_2={{CT:8}}\), so \(\frac{|v_1\cdot v_2|}{\|v_1\|\,\|v_2\|}=1\)):

\[ \cos\theta=1 \]

[[/if]]

on_true.feedback: Part a — correct. Yes this is the correct configuration of the two lines.

on_false.feedback: Part a — incorrect. You chose the wrong configuration.

on_true.feedback:
The first thing to note is that the direction vectors v1={{CT:26}} and v2={{CT:27}} are linearly independent. In the plane this means that the two lines must intersect.

For the future note that in \(R^3\) this is not the case anymore.

on_false.feedback:
The first thing to note is that the direction vectors \(v_1={{CT:1}}\) and \(v_2={{CT:3}}\) are linearly dependent. This means that the two lines are either parallel or coincident.

Even though the two lines do not come with the same parameterization they might still coincide. As shown in the first figure. However since we already determined that the lines are either coincident or parallel it would be enough to check one point. For example we can check if \(w_2={{CT:2}} \in \ell_1\) by solving the linear equation \(w_2 = w_1 + \alpha v_1\). Explicitly this is a system of two equations with one unknown \(\alpha\)

\[ {{CT:2}} = {{CT:0}} + \alpha {{CT:1}} \]

on_true.feedback: Since this equation has a solution we deduce that \(w_2 \in \ell_1\) and hence the two lines are coincident.

on_false.feedback: Since this equation does not have a solution we deduce that \(w_2 \not \in \ell_1\) and hence the two lines are parallel but not coincident.

on_true.feedback: Part b — correct. You calculated the distance between the lines correctly.

on_false.feedback: Part b — incorrect. You didn't calculate the distance between the lines correctly.

on_true.feedback: Since the two lines are intersecting, the distance between them must be zero.
Since the two lines coincide the distance between them must be zero.

on_false.feedback:
One way to do this is as follows. Since the two lines are parallel we can find a vector that is orthogonal to the directions of both lines. This can be done for example by applying rotation by 90 degrees to \(v_1\) as follows:

\[ o = {{CT:12}} {{CT:1}} = {{CT:13}} \]

Now as the following picture shows, projecting \(w_2-w_1\) on the orthogonal direction gives a vector whose length is just the distance between the two lines.

\[ dist = \left| \left| \frac{ (w_2-w_1)\cdot o}{o \cdot o} o \right| \right| = {{CT:16}} \]

on_true.feedback: Part c — correct. You calculated the cosine of the angle between the two lines correctly.
Part c — correct. You calculated the cosine of the angle between the two lines correctly.

on_false.feedback:
Part c — incorrect. Your calculation of the angle of the cosine is wrong. All you have to do here is use the inner product according to the formula:

\[ cos(\phi) = \frac{v_1 \cdot v_2}{||v_1|| ||v_2||} = {{CT:20}} \]
